standard.title: Percentages, decimals and fractions
standard.description: Recognise that 100% represents the complete whole and use percentages to describe, represent and compare relative size; connect familiar percentages to their decimal and fraction equivalents
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can express natural numbers as products of factors and recognise multiples (AC9M5N02). They have not yet used percentages as a representation or connected familiar percentages to decimal and fraction equivalents.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students recognise that 100% represents the whole and use percentages to describe, represent and compare relative size; connect familiar percentages to decimal and fraction equivalents.

nodes.label: 100% as the whole
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain that 100% represents the complete whole and describe parts of a whole as percentages.
nodes.minimum_width: Shade or mark a percentage of a 100-grid and write the percentage; explain that the total always equals 100%.
nodes.typical_width: Represent percentages on 100-grids, bar models and number lines; describe real-world part-whole situations as percentages.
wider: Use statistical data displays to read percentages in context
Connect to First Nations representations of proportional sharing in cultural contexts
success_criteria: Student shades a given percentage of a 100-grid correctly
Student explains that all parts of a whole sum to 100%

nodes.label: Familiar percentage–fraction–decimal connections
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can convert between familiar percentages (50%, 25%, 10%, 75%) and their fraction and decimal equivalents.
nodes.minimum_width: Convert between 50%, 25%, 10% and their fraction and decimal equivalents; explain the connection.
nodes.typical_width: Extend to 75%, 20%, 5%, 1% and connect to hundredths decimals; use all three representations interchangeably for familiar values.
wider: Build a percentage–fraction–decimal reference chart extending to 33⅓%, 12.5%

response_modes.reason: Fluent recall of familiar equivalences (50%=0.5=½) is the foundation for all percentage calculation. Students benefit from targeted practice before tackling novel percentages.
Students who only see abstract tables often fail to apply equivalences in context. Money, measurement and data contexts help cement the connections.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The equivalence landscape (percentage–fraction–decimal triple) is rich for advancing students; money and data application contexts extend meaningfully.
nodes.hinge_reason: Fluent equivalence recall is directly required by Node 3 — students who cannot convert between representations cannot evaluate whether percentage comparisons reference the same whole.
success_criteria: Student converts between familiar percentages and their fraction/decimal equivalents without error
Student represents the equivalence in at least two forms

nodes.label: Comparing relative size with percentages
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use percentages to compare the relative size of parts across different wholes.
nodes.minimum_width: Compare two percentages and identify which is larger; explain that comparison is valid because both reference the same whole (100%).
nodes.typical_width: Compare relative sizes across contexts (e.g. 60% of class A vs 45% of class B); recognise that percentage comparison is only valid when the whole is the same or specified.
wider: Analyse media reports that use percentages to compare populations of different sizes
Investigate misleading percentage comparisons and explain what additional information is needed

response_modes.reason: The 'same whole' constraint is a key conceptual hurdle. Varied contexts — some where comparison is valid, some where it isn't — help students develop the necessary critical lens.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Media analysis and misleading statistics give advancing students genuinely rich critical thinking territory.
success_criteria: Student correctly identifies which of two percentages represents a larger relative share
Student explains when percentage comparison is and is not valid
